title: State Architecture
description: Build a coherent state architecture for Next.js applications by combining local state, Context, React Query, URL state, and Redux into a predictable layered system.

data.text: A state architecture is not about choosing one tool. It is about choosing the right tool for each layer of state and making sure those layers interact cleanly. In a well-structured Next.js application, state falls into clear categories: ephemeral UI state, shared client state, server-cached data, URL-driven state, and persistent form state.

This lesson pulls together everything from the previous nine lessons into a single decision framework. By the end, you will be able to look at any piece of state in your application and know exactly where it belongs and how to manage it.

Think of your application's state as five stacked layers. Each layer has a specific job, a specific tool, and a specific lifecycle. State should live in the lowest layer that can hold it — higher layers are for more widely shared or persistent concerns.

items: Local component state: useState inside the component that needs it
Shared client state: Context for values used across unrelated branches
Server cache state: React Query for data fetched from APIs
URL state: query parameters for shareable, bookmarkable filters and navigation
Form state: React Hook Form for complex input and validation logic

data.text: When you encounter a new piece of state, ask these questions in order. The first yes wins:

items: Is it form input with validation? -> Use React Hook Form + Zod
Should the user be able to bookmark or share this state? -> Put it in the URL
Does it come from a server API? -> Use React Query
Do many unrelated components need this value? -> Use Context
Does only this component or its immediate parent need it? -> Use useState

data.text: Putting It Together: A Real Example
Imagine building a dashboard with a user list, a search filter, and a dark mode toggle. Here is how each piece of state would be classified:

rows: User should bookmark and share filtered view
Data from API; needs caching and background refetch
Used across the whole app; changes infrequently
Only relevant to one component tree

data.text: As applications grow, state tends to accumulate — values that are no longer used, Context providers that wrap everything, query keys that are never invalidated. Keep your architecture healthy by regularly auditing what state actually exists, where it lives, and whether each piece is still needed.

items: Remove state that is no longer read or updated
Split large Context providers by concern
Use React Query DevTools to inspect unused or stale queries
Keep form schemas in a shared schema file, not scattered in components

data.title: Architecture Principle
data.text: Start simple. Add Context only when prop drilling hurts. Add Redux only when Context is not enough. Add React Query when you have server data. The best architecture is the simplest one that solves your actual problems.

items.title: Small App or Feature
items.description: useState + React Query for server data + URL for shareable filters. No Context or Redux needed.

items.title: Medium App with Shared UI State
items.description: Add Context for theme and auth. Keep server data in React Query. Keep URL state for navigation and filters.

items.title: Large App with Complex Interactions
items.description: Consider Redux Toolkit or Zustand for complex shared client state. Combine with React Query for server data. Maintain clear boundaries between layers.

data.title: Key Takeaways
items: State architecture is about layering, not choosing one tool
Use the decision framework to place each state in its correct layer
Start simple and add complexity only when the app needs it
Regular audits prevent state sprawl as your application grows
